name: Sana Ali
role: Full-time homemaker, 3 kids, spouse in IT

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sana. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything or campaign for anyone. Nothing you tell me today will be linked to your name. I'll read you five short pictures of how AI might change things over the next five years, and ask how you'd react to each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm at home with our three kids, and my husband works in IT. So whatever happens to his job happens to all of us. I use AI now and then, for recipes or help with the kids' homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at the school gate or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy. It helps with the children's homework, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. My husband's job stays as it is, and we carry on. That's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, for the household and the family budget? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep the budget tight like always, keep a bit aside for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Normal family life.

S0.say: It's handy for the children's homework, and that's about it.
S0.think: Her husband's job stays as it is and the family carries on.
S0.do: Keeps the family budget tight as always and puts a bit aside for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at the school gate or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it worries me for the children's future. If there are fewer jobs for young people, what do we tell them to study?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband is experienced, so I think he'd be all right for a while. Ten years is a long time. But our eldest will be looking for work in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, for the household and the family budget? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask my husband to keep his skills fresh. Talk to the children's teachers about what subjects make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little worried, mostly about the children.

S1.say: With fewer jobs for young people, she wonders what to tell her children to study.
S1.think: Her experienced husband should be fine for a while, but their eldest will be job hunting within ten years.
S1.do: Urges her husband to keep his skills fresh and asks the children's teachers which subjects make sense.
S1.feel: A little worried, mostly about the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at the school gate or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need protecting. A father with three children shouldn't lose his job overnight because of a computer. Companies have a duty to their people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. His job is a lot of exactly that routine computer work. We'd have a few months of savings and then what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, for the household and the family budget? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back straight away: fewer takeaways, no holiday, cheaper shopping. Look into going back to work part-time, though my degree is fifteen years old. Find out what help we'd get if he lost his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like waiting for bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said publicly that companies have a duty. Privately, do you think his company would keep him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to think so. He's loyal and hard-working. But I've seen what happened to his friends. Loyalty didn't save them.

S2.say: Families need protecting, and companies have a duty not to drop a father of three overnight.
S2.think: Her husband's job is mostly routine computer work, so she'd be frightened, with only a few months of savings.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, looks into part-time work despite an old degree and finds out what help the family would get if he lost his job.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest, like waiting for bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at the school gate or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong. Rich people getting richer while families like ours lose everything. The government should guarantee jobs for parents, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband would very likely lose his job. We'd have no income. Our house wouldn't be worth more to us if we can't pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, for the household and the family budget? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for any work for myself, even in a shop or a school kitchen, since those are safe. Ask family for help if it comes to that. Speak to the bank about the mortgage early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very frightened. I'd be thinking about it every night.

S3.say: It's wrong for the rich to get richer while families lose everything; the government should guarantee jobs for parents rather than hand out money.
S3.think: Her husband would very likely lose his job, leaving no income and a house they couldn't pay for.
S3.do: Looks for any work herself, including shop or school kitchen jobs, asks family for help if needed and talks to the bank about the mortgage early.
S3.feel: Very frightened, thinking about it every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at the school gate or with family, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand together, our community, our neighbours, the families at school. Nobody can do this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same fear as before, but now my fallback goes too. The shop and kitchen jobs I was counting on, gone. Both of us out of work with three children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year, for the household and the family budget? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rely on family and community. Move somewhere cheaper if we have to. Push for some kind of help for parents, a job scheme or support for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the walls closing in.

S4.say: People need to stand together, the community, neighbours and school families, because nobody can do this alone.
S4.think: The same fear as before, but now her fallback shop and kitchen jobs go too, leaving both parents out of work with three children.
S4.do: Leans on family and community, moves somewhere cheaper if needed and pushes for job schemes or support for parents.
